opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the core idea behind MrT5 — which stands for MergeT5 — is that we add a learned deletion mechanism to ByT5's encoder. After a few early encoder layers, a small gating module decides which byte-level tokens can be dropped, and the remaining layers operate on that shorter sequence. So the efficiency gains really come down to how much we can shrink the sequence, and how early.

A few conditions matter most. The first is sequence length. Because self-attention scales quadratically, the savings from deleting tokens are much bigger on long inputs. For short inputs the gating overhead is small but so is the payoff; on longer documents you see substantial reductions in runtime.

The second is where the deletion happens. We place the gate fairly early, around layer three. By then the model has had enough context to merge information from neighboring bytes into the tokens it keeps, but most of the encoder still runs on the compressed sequence. Deleting too early hurts quality, and deleting too late leaves savings on the table.

The third is the deletion rate itself, which we can control with a regularizer, so there's a tunable tradeoff between compression and task performance. In our experiments we could delete a large fraction of tokens, often more than half and sometimes up to around 75%, with minimal loss in performance on things like XNLI and character-level tasks.

And the fourth is language and script. Byte-level encoding is very uneven across languages. Scripts that need multiple bytes per character are especially inflated in sequence length, and the model learns different deletion rates for different languages, essentially learning how compressible each one is. That makes it less of a fixed tokenizer and more of a context-sensitive, adaptive compression.

Finally, it's worth noting that the gains are on the encoder side. For tasks where the encoder dominates compute, like classification or generation with short outputs, you get the most benefit. Where the decoder does a lot of autoregressive work, the end-to-end speedup is smaller, though you still save on cross-attention because the decoder attends to a shorter encoder output.

r001.rationale: The response says gains are largest on long inputs and for tasks with short outputs where encoder compute dominates; it says decoder-heavy tasks have smaller end-to-end speedups.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. The big picture with MrT5 is that we're trying to fix the fundamental cost problem of byte-level models. ByT5 operates directly on raw bytes instead of subword tokens, which is great for robustness, for multilingual coverage, for handling things like typos or character-level tasks. But the sequence lengths are much longer than what a subword tokenizer would give you, and because self-attention scales quadratically, that gets expensive fast.

What MrT5 does is add a learned deletion gate after a few early encoder layers. So the first couple of layers process the full byte sequence and build up some contextual information, and then the gate decides which positions can be dropped. The remaining encoder layers, and the cross-attention in the decoder, only operate on the shortened sequence. The gate is trained with a regularizer that lets us dial in roughly how aggressive the deletion should be.

So to your question about when the gains are greatest, there are a few conditions that stand out.

The first is just how much redundancy there is in the input. Bytes are inherently redundant. A lot of positions in a byte sequence are predictable from their neighbors, think of the trailing bytes of a word once you've seen the first few characters. The more of that there is, the more the model can delete without losing information, and the bigger the speedup.

The second, and this is one of the more interesting findings, is the language. Byte-level models have this fairness problem where languages that use multi-byte UTF-8 encodings, so scripts like Cyrillic, Arabic, or CJK characters, end up with sequences two to four times longer than English for the same content. That means they pay a much higher compute cost. What we saw with MrT5 is that it learns language-specific deletion rates. It deletes more aggressively on those languages, because there's more redundancy within the multi-byte characters, and so the efficiency gains are actually larger for exactly the languages that were being penalized most. It partially closes that gap.

The third factor is sequence length more broadly. Since the savings come from shrinking what the later layers and the decoder attend over, longer inputs benefit more in absolute terms. On short inputs the overhead of the gate and the early full-length layers takes up a larger share of the total.

And then there's the deletion ratio you choose. We found you can delete somewhere around half the sequence, and in some settings substantially more, with minimal accuracy loss on downstream tasks. If you push the regularizer harder, you get more speed but you start trading off quality, so the sweet spot depends on your task tolerance.

The one caveat I'd add is that the efficiency win is in the encoder and in cross-attention. The decoder's self-attention still generates byte by byte, so for tasks with very long outputs, that part of the cost doesn't change. The biggest gains are really on tasks with long, redundant inputs, especially in non-Latin scripts, and relatively short outputs.

r001.rationale: The response says the biggest gains occur with long inputs and relatively short outputs, explaining that long inputs benefit from encoder sequence shortening while long decoder outputs leave more cost unchanged.

astra-6.text:
I’d frame it in terms of how much the model can shorten the byte sequence, and how much computation remains after it does that. ByT5 operates on bytes throughout, so it can spend a lot of computation on very long sequences. Mr. T5 learns to delete some positions and pass a shorter representation to the later layers.

The biggest gains come when it can compress that sequence substantially without losing information the task needs. Longer inputs offer more opportunity, especially when much of the cost is in processing the encoder sequence. But the deletion rate alone doesn’t tell you the end-to-end speedup: you still pay for the layers before deletion, and if generating a long output dominates runtime, shortening the input has a smaller relative effect. So the key is the combination of useful compression, preserved task performance, and where the computation is actually being spent.

r001.rationale: The response says gains are greatest with longer inputs when encoder processing is costly, and that long-output generation reduces the relative benefit. This conveys that gains are strongest when encoder sequences are long relative to decoder sequences.

sol-6.1.text:
The key is whether the savings from shortening the sequence outweigh the cost of deciding which tokens to merge. Mr. T5 starts with bytes, like ByT5, but learns to merge representations so that later encoder layers operate on a shorter sequence. That helps most when the input is long and the model can merge it fairly aggressively without losing information needed for the task.

The other piece is how much of inference is spent in the encoder versus the decoder. If you have a long input and a relatively short output, reducing the encoder sequence length can make a substantial difference. If you're generating a long output, autoregressive decoding can dominate the runtime, so the overall gain is smaller. So sequence compression is the mechanism, but input length, output length, and the amount of merging you can tolerate determine the actual speedup.

r001.rationale: The response says gains are substantial with a long input and relatively short output, because shortening the encoder sequence matters more when decoder generation is brief.
